section-4: The word 'curriculum' comes from the Latin word 'currere', meaning 'to run' or 'a racecourse'. Cunningham described it as a tool in the hands of the artist (teacher) to mould his material (pupil) according to his ideal (objective) in his studio (school). The Secondary Education Commission (1952-53) stated that curriculum includes the totality of experiences that pupils receive through the manifold activities in school, classroom, library, laboratory, workshop and playground.
Curriculum is wider than syllabus. The syllabus is a list of topics to be taught in a subject, whereas the curriculum includes objectives, content, methods, co-curricular activities and evaluation.
section-5: Functions: (1) translating educational aims into concrete learning experiences; (2) providing a framework for teachers; (3) promoting all-round development - physical, intellectual, emotional, social and moral; (4) transmitting culture; (5) preparing learners for life and vocations; (6) meeting individual differences; (7) promoting national integration and democratic values.
A good curriculum also serves as a basis for evaluation and helps maintain uniform standards across schools.
section-6: Main types: (1) subject-centred curriculum - organised around separate subjects; (2) learner/child-centred curriculum - based on needs and interests of the child; (3) activity or experience-centred curriculum - learning through activities (Dewey); (4) core curriculum - common essential subjects for all, with electives; (5) integrated curriculum - combining related subjects around themes; (6) broad-fields curriculum - grouping related subjects (e.g. social studies).

Other concepts include the hidden curriculum (unplanned values and attitudes learned in school), the null curriculum (what is not taught) and the spiral curriculum (Bruner), where topics are revisited with increasing complexity.
section-7: Earlier they were called extra-curricular activities, but now they are considered part of the curriculum. Types include literary activities (debates, quizzes, magazines), cultural activities (music, dance, drama), physical activities (games, sports, yoga), social service (NSS, NCC, scouts and guides, community service), scientific activities (science clubs, exhibitions) and excursions.

Values: they develop personality, leadership, cooperation, discipline, creativity, physical fitness, use of leisure time and social skills. Teachers should plan them properly and ensure participation of all students.
section-8: An undifferentiated curriculum is common at the elementary stage, where all children study the same core subjects such as languages, mathematics, environmental studies and arts. It provides a common foundation of knowledge, skills and values.

Advantages: promotes equality, social cohesion and a common culture; simple to administer. Limitations: it may not meet individual differences in abilities, interests and aptitudes, and may not prepare students for specialised careers.
section-9: A differentiated curriculum is introduced at the higher secondary and higher education levels, where students choose streams (science, arts, commerce, vocational) or electives. It is also used for gifted children, slow learners and children with special needs.

Advantages: caters to individual differences, develops special talents, prepares for vocations and higher studies. Limitations: early specialisation may narrow general education, and it requires guidance and more resources. NEP 2020 recommends flexibility in subject choices without rigid separation of streams.
section-10: Important principles: (1) child-centredness - based on the needs, interests and abilities of learners; (2) community-centredness - related to social needs; (3) activity-centredness; (4) principle of utility; (5) principle of flexibility; (6) principle of variety and balance; (7) principle of integration and correlation; (8) principle of preparation for life; (9) principle of conservation and creativity - preserving culture while promoting new ideas; (10) principle of forward-looking (future needs).
The curriculum should also promote national values, democratic citizenship and the use of leisure time.
section-11: Situational analysis is the first step in curriculum development (Skilbeck's model). It examines external factors (social and cultural changes, parental and employer expectations, educational policies, research, technology) and internal factors (learners' abilities and needs, teachers' skills, school resources, existing curriculum problems).
It ensures that the curriculum is realistic, relevant and suited to the actual context. Methods include surveys, interviews, observation, document analysis and SWOT analysis.
section-12: Objectives may be general (aims of education) or specific (instructional objectives stated in behavioural terms). Bloom's taxonomy (1956) classified objectives into cognitive (knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, evaluation), affective (receiving, responding, valuing, organisation, characterisation) and psychomotor domains. The revised taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl, 2001) uses remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate and create.
Good objectives are clear, specific, measurable, achievable, relevant to learners and society, and consistent with national goals of education.
section-13: Criteria for selecting content (Tyler, Taba and others): validity (accurate and up to date), significance (important ideas and concepts), interest, utility, learnability (suited to learners' level), feasibility (time and resources available) and consistency with social realities.
Content should cover knowledge, skills and values and avoid overloading. It should include local and national context, as recommended by NCF 2005 (connecting knowledge to life outside school).
section-14: Ralph Tyler identified three criteria for organising learning experiences: continuity (repetition of important elements), sequence (each experience builds on the previous one, from simple to complex) and integration (horizontal relationship between subjects).

Approaches include logical vs psychological organisation, topical and concentric organisation, spiral organisation, chronological organisation (in history) and correlation of subjects. Good organisation helps understanding and transfer of learning.
section-15: Curriculum evaluation examines whether the curriculum's objectives are achieved, whether content and methods are appropriate and whether resources are used efficiently. Models include Tyler's objectives model, Stufflebeam's CIPP model (Context, Input, Process, Product) and Scriven's goal-free evaluation.
It helps in improving the curriculum, making decisions about continuation or change, accountability and providing feedback to teachers, administrators and policymakers.
section-16: Tools: achievement tests and diagnostic tests (to measure learning outcomes), questionnaires and opinion surveys (for teachers, students, parents), observation schedules and checklists (classroom processes), interviews, rating scales, attitude scales, cumulative records, anecdotal records, portfolios and analysis of textbooks and documents.
A combination of quantitative and qualitative tools gives a more complete picture of the curriculum's effectiveness.
section-17: The terms formative and summative evaluation were introduced by Michael Scriven (1967). Formative evaluation is continuous and diagnostic: it identifies weaknesses during the try-out stage, pilot testing or teaching so that changes can be made in time.
Examples: trying out new textbooks in a few schools, collecting feedback from teachers and students during the year, and class tests. It is mainly for improvement rather than judgement.
section-18: Summative evaluation is final and judgemental. It determines the overall worth, effectiveness and outcomes of a curriculum and helps decide whether it should be continued, modified or replaced.

Examples: board examinations, end-of-year achievement surveys like the National Achievement Survey, and comprehensive reviews of curriculum after several years. It is used for accountability and certification.
section-19: Criteria: (1) content - accurate, up to date, relevant to syllabus and free from bias; (2) organisation - logical sequence, clear chapters, summaries and exercises; (3) language - simple, clear and suited to learners' age; (4) illustrations - relevant pictures, diagrams and maps; (5) activities and exercises - promoting thinking and application; (6) physical features - quality of printing, paper, binding and size; (7) values - promotes national integration, gender equality and constitutional values.
Evaluation can be done using checklists and rating scales by teachers, experts and students. NCERT has developed guidelines for textbook evaluation.
section-20: Curriculum change may be minor (updating a topic) or major (complete reform, such as NCF 2005 or NCF-SE 2023). It may be initiated from the top (government policies) or from the bottom (school-based initiatives).
Stages of change include initiation (identifying need), planning, development of new materials, implementation (including teacher training), and evaluation and institutionalisation.
section-21: Conditions for successful change: a felt need for change, clear goals, involvement of stakeholders (teachers, parents, students, experts), adequate resources and infrastructure, teacher training and orientation, administrative and political support, pilot testing, effective communication and continuous evaluation.
Resistance to change can arise from fear of the unknown, lack of skills, workload and vested interests; it can be reduced through participation, training and support.
section-22: Factors: social and cultural changes, explosion of knowledge, technological changes (computers, internet), economic needs and employment patterns, political ideology and national policies (such as NEP 2020), globalisation, research in psychology and learning, demands of parents and employers, and environmental issues.
Barriers include lack of funds, rigid examination systems, inadequate teacher preparation, large class sizes and resistance from teachers or parents.
section-23: Teachers: they are the key implementers; they interpret the curriculum, adapt it to local needs, give feedback, write materials and participate in curriculum committees. Their training and attitude decide success. Students: their needs and feedback guide change; they participate through surveys and student councils.
Administrators (principals, education officers, boards, SCERT, NCERT): they plan, provide resources, organise training, monitor implementation and create a supportive climate for innovation.
section-25: Concept: Curriculum is the total of planned learning experiences - subjects, activities, co-curricular programmes and school life - through which educational aims are realised. It is broader than the syllabus and includes objectives, content, methods and evaluation.
Functions: It translates aims into practice, guides teachers, promotes all-round development, transmits culture, prepares for life and vocations, and supports national goals.

Types: Subject-centred, child-centred, activity-centred, core, integrated, broad-fields and spiral curricula, as well as the hidden and null curriculum. Undifferentiated curricula provide common learning for all, especially at the elementary stage; differentiated curricula offer choices according to abilities and interests at higher stages.

Co-curricular activities: Literary, cultural, physical, social and scientific activities are integral to the curriculum because they develop personality, leadership, creativity and social skills. A balanced curriculum combines academic and co-curricular experiences.
section-26: Principles of construction: The curriculum should be child-centred, community-centred, activity-based, flexible, balanced, integrated, useful, forward-looking and consistent with national values.

Steps of construction (Tyler and Taba models): (1) situational analysis of learners, society and resources; (2) selection of objectives using Bloom's taxonomy; (3) selection of content based on validity, significance, interest, utility and learnability; (4) organisation of content with continuity, sequence and integration; (5) selection and organisation of learning experiences and methods; (6) evaluation.
Organisation: Content may be organised logically or psychologically, topically, concentrically or spirally. Integration across subjects and correlation with life make learning meaningful.
Conclusion: Systematic curriculum construction ensures that the curriculum is relevant, realistic and effective in achieving educational goals.
section-27: Meaning: Curriculum evaluation is the systematic process of collecting information to judge the value and effectiveness of a curriculum and to improve it.
Models: Tyler's objectives-based model, Stufflebeam's CIPP model (context, input, process, product) and Scriven's goal-free model are well known.
Instruments: Tests, questionnaires, interviews, observation, rating scales, checklists, records and document analysis provide information about learning outcomes and processes.

Formative and summative evaluation: Formative evaluation is conducted during development and implementation to improve the curriculum; summative evaluation is conducted at the end to judge overall worth. Textbook evaluation using criteria of content, organisation, language, illustrations, activities and physical features is an important part of curriculum evaluation.
section-28: Meaning: Curriculum change is the modification of aims, content, methods, materials or evaluation in response to new needs. It may be minor or major, top-down or bottom-up.
Factors: Social and cultural change, knowledge explosion, technology, economic needs, political decisions and national policies, globalisation and research on learning drive curriculum change.
Conditions for success: Felt need, clear objectives, participation of stakeholders, resources, teacher training, administrative support, pilot testing and evaluation.

Roles: Teachers implement and adapt the curriculum; students provide feedback; administrators plan, support and monitor. Resistance to change must be managed through communication and support. Recent examples include NCF 2005, NEP 2020 and NCF-SE 2023 in India.
section-31: Definitions: Jones - guidance is the help given by one person to another in making choices and adjustments and in solving problems. Crow and Crow - guidance is assistance made available by competent counsellors to an individual of any age to help him direct his own life, develop his own point of view, make his own decisions and carry his own burdens.

Characteristics: guidance is a continuous process, it is help and not imposition, it aims at self-direction and self-realisation, and it is meant for all individuals, not only for those with problems.
section-32: Need from the educational point of view: choice of subjects and courses, adjustment to school, study habits, prevention of wastage and stagnation. Vocational point of view: choice of suitable careers, knowledge of the world of work and changing job market. Personal point of view: emotional adjustment, adolescent problems, stress and peer pressure.
Social point of view: rapid social change, breakdown of joint families, unemployment, drug abuse and use of leisure. National point of view: proper use of human resources for national development.
section-33: Principles: (1) guidance is for all; (2) it is based on individual differences; (3) it respects the dignity and worth of the individual; (4) it is continuous and lifelong; (5) it is a cooperative process involving teachers, parents and counsellors; (6) it is based on reliable data about the individual; (7) it aims at self-guidance; (8) it should be flexible and adapted to needs; (9) it should be evaluated periodically.
Guidance should not impose decisions but help the individual make his or her own choices.
section-34: Educational guidance helps students choose suitable subjects, courses and institutions according to their abilities and interests, develop effective study habits, adjust to school, deal with examinations and learning difficulties, and plan for higher education.
It is especially important at transitional stages, such as after Class VIII, Class X and Class XII. Tools include aptitude tests, achievement records, interest inventories and cumulative records.
section-35: Frank Parsons is regarded as the father of vocational guidance; he established the Vocation Bureau in Boston in 1908. His approach involves (1) understanding oneself, (2) knowledge of occupations, and (3) matching the two through 'true reasoning'.

Vocational guidance includes career information, career talks, career fairs, visits to industries, aptitude testing and placement services. It reduces wrong career choices, frustration and unemployment and helps the nation use its human resources effectively.
section-36: Personal guidance deals with problems such as emotional difficulties, anxiety, lack of confidence, family conflicts, peer relationships, adolescent problems, health and hygiene, and use of leisure time.
Its aim is to help the individual develop a well-adjusted, integrated personality. It is provided through counselling, group discussions, life-skills education and cooperation with parents.
section-37: Educational guidance focuses on academic success and choices; vocational guidance focuses on career choice and preparation; personal guidance focuses on emotional and social well-being. They are interrelated: a student's personal problems may affect studies and career choice, and wrong subject choice may cause emotional problems.
Therefore, a comprehensive guidance programme in schools includes all three types and is provided by trained counsellors with the help of teachers and parents.
section-38: Job analysis results in two documents: the job description (duties, responsibilities, working conditions, tools used) and the job specification (qualifications, skills, physical and mental abilities, experience and personal qualities required).
It is used in vocational guidance, recruitment and selection, training, performance appraisal, wage fixation and improving working conditions.
section-39: Methods: (1) observation - watching workers at work; (2) interview - with workers and supervisors; (3) questionnaire - written answers about duties; (4) work diary or log - workers record daily activities; (5) critical incident technique - recording effective and ineffective behaviour; (6) records and documents; (7) technical conferences with experts; (8) participation - analyst performs the job himself.
Usually a combination of methods is used for accurate results.
section-40: Importance: it provides accurate occupational information for career guidance; helps in matching the right person to the right job; aids recruitment, selection and placement; identifies training needs; helps in fixing fair wages; improves safety and working conditions; and is used in performance appraisal.
For students, job analysis information helps them understand what different careers actually involve, so they can make realistic choices.
section-41: Uses: preparation of career literature, vocational guidance, selection and placement, training programmes, job evaluation and salary fixation, and organisational planning.

Limitations: it is time-consuming and costly; jobs change rapidly due to technology; workers may give inaccurate information; it may ignore personal and social aspects of work; and it requires trained analysts.
section-42: Locke defined job satisfaction as a pleasurable or positive emotional state resulting from the appraisal of one's job or job experiences. High job satisfaction leads to better performance, commitment and mental health, and lower absenteeism and turnover.

Herzberg's two-factor theory distinguishes motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth) that create satisfaction and hygiene factors (pay, working conditions, supervision, policies) that prevent dissatisfaction.
section-43: Personal factors: age, sex, education, personality, aspirations, and match between abilities and job. Job-related factors: nature of work, salary, security, promotion opportunities, working conditions, recognition, autonomy, relations with colleagues and superiors, and organisational policies.
Teachers' job satisfaction is particularly important because it affects their teaching effectiveness and students' learning.
section-44: Definitions: Carl Rogers described counselling as a series of direct contacts with the individual which aims to offer him assistance in changing his attitudes and behaviour. Wrenn described it as a dynamic and purposeful relationship between two people.

Counselling is the heart of the guidance programme. It involves a trained counsellor and a client, a confidential relationship, two-way communication and the aim of helping the client make decisions and solve problems. Stages include establishing rapport, exploring the problem, setting goals, action and termination/follow-up.
section-45: Principles: (1) acceptance of the client without judgement; (2) respect for the individual; (3) confidentiality; (4) client's self-determination - decisions are made by the client; (5) empathy and understanding; (6) permissiveness - freedom to express feelings; (7) counselling is a learning process; (8) it should be based on adequate information; (9) the counsellor should be competent and ethical.
Following these principles builds trust and makes counselling effective.
section-46: Directive (counsellor-centred) counselling was developed by E.G. Williamson. The counsellor plays the main role, gathers information, diagnoses the problem and advises the client. Steps: analysis, synthesis, diagnosis, prognosis, counselling and follow-up.

Merits: saves time, useful for intellectual and educational problems, and for clients who need guidance. Limitations: the client becomes dependent, it ignores emotions and may not help in personal problems.
section-47: Non-directive (client-centred) counselling was developed by Carl Rogers. The counsellor creates a warm, accepting and permissive atmosphere, listens empathetically and reflects feelings, while the client takes responsibility for understanding the problem and making decisions.

Merits: promotes self-understanding, independence and emotional growth; suitable for personal and emotional problems. Limitations: time-consuming, may not suit immature clients or urgent problems, and requires skilled counsellors.
section-48: Eclectic counselling was advocated by F.C. Thorne. It combines directive and non-directive techniques according to the needs of the client and the nature of the problem. The counsellor may begin non-directively to build rapport and then become directive when information or advice is needed.
Merits: flexible, practical and suited to different situations. Limitation: requires a highly skilled counsellor who can judge when to use which approach.
section-49: Essential skills: active listening, empathy, building rapport, questioning (open and closed), reflecting feelings, paraphrasing and summarising, observation of non-verbal behaviour, problem-solving and decision-making skills, and knowledge of tests and techniques.
Personal qualities: warmth, patience, sincerity, emotional maturity, objectivity, respect for confidentiality, ethical behaviour and cultural sensitivity.
section-50: Testing techniques: intelligence tests, aptitude tests (DAT), achievement tests, interest inventories (Strong, Kuder), personality inventories and attitude scales. Non-testing techniques: interview, observation, cumulative record cards, anecdotal records, case studies, autobiography, rating scales and sociometry.
These tools give reliable information about the individual's abilities, interests and personality, which is necessary for effective guidance and counselling.
section-52: Meaning: Guidance is a continuous process of helping individuals to understand themselves and their environment and to make wise choices and adjustments in educational, vocational and personal matters.

Need: Individual differences in abilities and interests, complexity of courses and careers, adolescent problems, social change, unemployment, wastage and stagnation in education, and the need to use human resources properly.
Principles: Guidance is for all, continuous, based on individual differences and reliable data, respects the dignity and freedom of the individual, is cooperative and aims at self-direction.

Organisation in schools: A good guidance programme includes orientation, testing, counselling, information services, placement and follow-up, carried out by counsellors with the help of teachers, parents and the community.
section-53: Educational guidance: Helps students choose subjects and courses, improve study habits, adjust to school and plan for further studies, especially at transition points.
Vocational guidance: Based on Frank Parsons' approach of matching self-knowledge with occupational knowledge, it provides career information, aptitude testing, career talks and placement services.
Personal guidance: Helps individuals with emotional, social, health and family problems and supports personality development.

Interrelationship: These types overlap and support each other. A comprehensive school guidance programme addresses all three areas to ensure academic success, suitable career choice and healthy personal adjustment.
section-54: Job analysis: A systematic study of a job to determine its tasks, responsibilities, working conditions and the skills and qualities required, producing a job description and job specification.

Methods and uses: Observation, interview, questionnaire, diaries, critical incidents and records are used. Job analysis is valuable in vocational guidance, recruitment, training, performance appraisal and wage fixation. Its limitations include cost, time and rapid changes in jobs.

Job satisfaction: Job satisfaction is the positive feeling a person has toward work. It is influenced by pay, security, nature of work, recognition, promotion, working conditions and relationships. Herzberg's two-factor theory distinguishes motivators and hygiene factors.

Importance in guidance: Matching people to suitable jobs increases job satisfaction, productivity and mental health. Thus job analysis and understanding of job satisfaction are essential components of vocational guidance.
section-55: Meaning: Counselling is a professional, confidential relationship in which a trained counsellor helps a client understand problems, explore options and make decisions.

Approaches: Directive counselling (Williamson) is counsellor-centred and suitable for educational and vocational problems; non-directive counselling (Rogers) is client-centred and suitable for emotional problems; eclectic counselling (Thorne) combines both according to the situation.

Principles and skills: Acceptance, respect, confidentiality, empathy, self-determination and permissiveness are key principles. Skills include active listening, questioning, reflecting, summarising and observation; personal qualities include warmth, patience and ethics.

Tests and techniques: Intelligence, aptitude, achievement, interest and personality tests, along with interviews, observation, cumulative records and case studies, provide information for effective counselling.
section-58: The WHO defines mental health as a state of well-being in which an individual realises his or her own abilities, can cope with the normal stresses of life, can work productively and is able to make a contribution to the community.

Mental health is not merely the absence of mental illness. It includes emotional maturity, realistic self-concept, social adjustment and a purposeful life. Good mental health is necessary for effective learning and teaching.
section-59: The mental hygiene movement was started by Clifford Beers, whose book 'A Mind That Found Itself' (1908) described his experiences in mental hospitals. Mental hygiene includes preventive, preservative and curative aspects.

In schools, mental hygiene involves a healthy environment, friendly teacher-pupil relations, avoidance of excessive pressure, guidance and counselling services, and early identification of emotional problems.
section-60: Objectives: (1) preservation of mental health; (2) prevention of mental disorders; (3) cure (early treatment) of mental illness; (4) development of an integrated personality; (5) promotion of healthy adjustment in family, school and society; (6) creating awareness about mental health.
For teachers, mental hygiene aims at maintaining both their own mental health and that of their students.
section-61: Parenting styles described by Diana Baumrind include authoritative (warm and firm - best for mental health), authoritarian (strict and controlling), permissive (indulgent) and neglectful. Children of authoritative parents tend to be confident, responsible and well-adjusted.

Harmful practices include overprotection, rejection, excessive punishment, inconsistent discipline, comparison with siblings and broken homes. Love, security, acceptance, appropriate freedom and positive discipline promote mental health.
section-62: Stress arises from demands that exceed one's coping capacity; frustration arises when goals are blocked; conflict arises from incompatible choices. Negative self-concept, feelings of inferiority, anxiety, guilt and fear can disturb mental health.

Positive psychological factors such as self-esteem, optimism, emotional intelligence, resilience and a sense of purpose protect mental health. Schools can develop these through life-skills education and counselling.
section-63: Characteristics of a wholesome (integrated) personality: realistic self-understanding and self-acceptance, emotional maturity, social adjustment and respect for others, a sense of responsibility, a positive philosophy of life, ability to face reality, self-confidence and consistency in behaviour.
Such a personality develops through healthy home and school environments, balanced physical, intellectual, emotional, social and moral development, and opportunities for self-expression.
section-64: Abnormality can be judged by statistical deviation from the average, violation of social norms, personal distress and maladaptive behaviour that interferes with daily life. Examples include anxiety disorders, depression, phobias, obsessive-compulsive disorder and personality disorders.

Causes may be biological (heredity, brain chemistry), psychological (traumatic experiences, faulty learning, conflicts) and social (poverty, family disorganisation, discrimination). Early identification and treatment are important.
section-65: Traditional classification: neuroses (milder disorders where contact with reality is maintained, e.g. anxiety, phobia, hysteria, obsessive-compulsive disorder) and psychoses (severe disorders with loss of contact with reality, e.g. schizophrenia and bipolar disorder).

Modern classifications are DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association) and ICD-11 (World Health Organization). Categories include anxiety disorders, mood disorders, neurodevelopmental disorders (ADHD, autism), personality disorders, substance-related disorders and psychotic disorders.
section-66: Characteristics according to Jahoda and others: positive attitude towards self, growth and self-actualisation, integration of personality, autonomy, accurate perception of reality and environmental mastery.

Such a person can handle stress, enjoy work and leisure, form satisfying relationships, accept responsibilities and adapt to change. Teachers with good mental health create positive classroom climates.
section-67: Play therapy was developed by Anna Freud, Melanie Klein and Virginia Axline. Children often cannot express feelings in words, so they express their anxieties, fears and conflicts through play with toys, dolls, sand, clay, drawing and puppets.
The therapist observes the play and helps the child understand and resolve emotional problems. It is useful for children who have experienced trauma, abuse, anxiety or behavioural problems.
section-68: Behaviour therapy is based on the learning theories of Pavlov, Watson and Skinner. It holds that abnormal behaviour is learned and can be unlearned. Techniques include systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) for phobias, positive reinforcement, token economy, modelling, aversion therapy and behaviour modification.
In schools it is used to reduce problem behaviours such as aggression, inattention and truancy and to develop desirable habits through reinforcement.
section-69: Counselling therapy includes approaches like client-centred therapy (Carl Rogers), cognitive-behavioural therapy (Aaron Beck, Albert Ellis's REBT) and group counselling. It helps individuals express their feelings, gain insight and develop coping strategies.
It is useful for students with stress, anxiety, adjustment problems, low self-esteem, relationship issues and career confusion.
section-70: According to Gates and others, adjustment is a continual process by which a person varies his behaviour to produce a more harmonious relationship between himself and his environment. A well-adjusted person satisfies needs in socially acceptable ways.
Areas of adjustment include home, school, health, social and emotional adjustment. Signs of good adjustment are emotional balance, social acceptance, academic success and realistic goals.
section-71: Symptoms of maladjustment include aggression, withdrawal, anxiety, truancy, lying, stealing, poor academic performance, temper tantrums, excessive day-dreaming and nervous habits such as nail-biting.
Maladjusted children need understanding, guidance and counselling rather than punishment. Teachers should identify such children early and work with parents and counsellors.
section-72: Home factors: broken homes, parental conflict, rejection, over-protection, poverty, harsh discipline and comparison with siblings. School factors: rigid discipline, heavy curriculum, examination pressure, unsympathetic teachers, bullying and failure. Personal factors: physical defects, poor health, low intelligence or giftedness without challenge.
Social factors include bad company, peer pressure, mass media influence, social discrimination and unemployment.
section-73: Sigmund Freud and Anna Freud described defence mechanisms that operate largely unconsciously. Examples: repression (pushing painful thoughts out of awareness), rationalisation (giving reasonable excuses), projection (attributing one's faults to others), displacement (redirecting emotions to a safer target), regression (returning to childish behaviour), sublimation (channelling impulses into socially acceptable activities), compensation and identification.
Moderate use helps reduce anxiety, but excessive use prevents facing reality. Direct methods like problem-solving, increasing effort or changing goals are healthier.
section-74: Mental conflict causes tension, anxiety and indecision. If not resolved, it may lead to frustration and maladjustment.
It is common among adolescents who face choices about studies, careers, friendships and values.
section-75: Kurt Lewin's types: approach-approach conflict (two desirable goals), avoidance-avoidance conflict (two undesirable goals), approach-avoidance conflict (a goal with both attractive and unattractive aspects), and double approach-avoidance conflict.
Causes include incompatible motives, moral conflicts between desires and values, conflicting demands of parents and peers, high aspirations with low ability, and social and economic pressures.
section-76: Remedies: understanding the problem clearly, gathering information, weighing alternatives, making realistic decisions, seeking guidance and counselling, developing a clear set of values, setting achievable goals, learning stress management and relaxation, and participating in recreational activities.
Parents and teachers should provide a supportive environment and avoid placing contradictory demands on children.
section-78: Mental health: Mental health is a state of well-being in which a person can realise abilities, cope with stress, work productively and contribute to the community (WHO). It includes emotional balance, social adjustment and a realistic self-concept.

Mental hygiene: Started by Clifford Beers, mental hygiene is the science of preserving mental health and preventing mental illness. Its objectives are preservation, prevention, cure and development of integrated personality.
Child rearing and mental health: Authoritative parenting, love, security and consistent discipline promote mental health, while rejection, over-protection and harsh punishment harm it.

Psychological factors: Stress, frustration, conflict, anxiety and low self-esteem endanger mental health, while resilience, optimism and emotional intelligence protect it. Schools can promote mental hygiene through a healthy environment, counselling and life-skills education.
section-79: Wholesome personality: An integrated personality shows realistic self-understanding, emotional maturity, social adjustment, responsibility and a positive outlook on life.
Abnormal personality: Abnormality is judged by deviation from norms, distress and maladaptive behaviour. Causes are biological, psychological and social.

Classification: Behaviour disorders are traditionally classified into neuroses and psychoses; modern systems such as DSM-5 and ICD-11 classify anxiety, mood, neurodevelopmental, personality, psychotic and substance-related disorders.

Mentally healthy person: Such a person accepts self, perceives reality accurately, has autonomy and environmental mastery, maintains good relationships and adapts to change. Teachers should promote these qualities among students.
section-80: Play therapy: Through toys, drawing, sand and puppets, children express feelings they cannot verbalise. The therapist helps the child understand and resolve emotional conflicts. It is effective for anxiety, trauma and behaviour problems in young children.

Behaviour therapy: Based on learning principles, it uses reinforcement, systematic desensitisation, token economy, modelling and behaviour modification to replace maladaptive behaviours with adaptive ones.
Counselling therapy: Client-centred, cognitive-behavioural and group counselling help individuals gain insight, change thinking patterns and develop coping skills.

Role of the teacher: Teachers can identify children with emotional difficulties, refer them to counsellors, cooperate with parents and use simple behavioural techniques and play activities in the classroom.
section-81: Adjustment: Adjustment is the process of balancing one's needs with environmental demands. A well-adjusted person shows emotional balance, social acceptance and realistic goals.

Maladjustment: It appears as aggression, withdrawal, anxiety, truancy and poor performance. Causes lie in the home (conflict, rejection), school (pressure, failure, harsh discipline), individual (health, ability) and society (bad company, media, discrimination).

Adjustment mechanisms: Defence mechanisms like repression, rationalisation, projection, displacement, regression, sublimation and compensation reduce anxiety but should not replace direct problem-solving.

Mental conflict: Lewin's approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance and approach-avoidance conflicts cause tension. Remedies include clear values, realistic decisions, guidance, counselling and stress management.
section-85: Sparta was a military state where the aim of education was to produce strong, brave soldiers and obedient citizens. The state controlled education; weak infants were rejected. At the age of seven boys were sent to state barracks (agoge), where they received hard physical training, endurance tests, wrestling, running and military drills until about 30.

Girls also received physical training to become healthy mothers of strong soldiers. Intellectual and literary education was minimal. Spartan education produced discipline and patriotism but neglected individuality and culture.
section-86: Athenian education aimed at the harmonious development of body and mind and the preparation of good citizens for a democratic state. Education was private but supervised by the state. Boys studied at the palaestra (physical training) and the didascaleum (music, literature, poetry of Homer).

From 18 to 20 they received military and civic training (ephebic training). Later, philosophers like Socrates, Plato and Aristotle developed higher education. Girls were educated at home. Athens made a great contribution to the ideal of liberal education.
section-87: In early Rome, the family was the main agency of education; the father taught his son farming, warfare, religion, law (the Twelve Tables, learned by heart) and Roman virtues such as piety, obedience, courage and honesty. The mother trained children in early years.
Education was practical and aimed at producing a good farmer, soldier and citizen. There were few formal schools; learning took place through apprenticeship and imitation of elders.
section-88: After contact with Greece, Rome developed a three-tier school system: the ludus (elementary school for reading, writing and arithmetic), the grammar school (Latin and Greek grammar and literature) and the rhetoric school (oratory for public life and law).

Quintilian's 'Institutes of Oratory' described the ideal orator as a good man skilled in speaking. Roman education contributed Latin language and literature, law and a system of schools to later Europe. It declined with the fall of the Western Roman Empire; Emperor Justinian closed the philosophical schools in 529 AD.
section-89: Monasticism began with St. Benedict, who founded the monastery at Monte Cassino in 529 AD and gave the Benedictine Rule of work and prayer. Monasteries had schools for future monks (internal schools) and sometimes for outsiders (external schools).

Curriculum included reading, writing, Latin, religious texts, music for church services and later the seven liberal arts (trivium: grammar, rhetoric, logic; quadrivium: arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music). Monks copied and preserved manuscripts, keeping learning alive during the Dark Ages.
section-90: Scholasticism flourished from the 11th to the 14th century. Its leading thinkers were Anselm, Peter Abelard and St. Thomas Aquinas, whose 'Summa Theologica' combined Christian theology with Aristotle's philosophy.

Methods included lectures on authoritative texts, commentaries and disputations (debates). Scholasticism developed logical reasoning and contributed to the rise of universities, but it was criticised for being too abstract and dependent on authority.
section-91: Universities grew out of cathedral schools and guilds of teachers and students ('universitas'). Early universities included Bologna (law), Paris (theology), Salerno (medicine), Oxford and Cambridge.

They had faculties of arts, theology, law and medicine, granted degrees (bachelor, master, doctor), enjoyed privileges like self-government and freedom from taxes, and used lectures and disputations. They laid the foundation of modern higher education and academic freedom.
section-92: Chivalry was the education of the feudal nobility. A boy served as a page (7-14 years) in a lord's castle, learning manners, music, religion and service to ladies; then as a squire (14-21 years), learning horse riding, use of arms, hunting and attending the knight; at 21 he was knighted in a religious ceremony.

The ideals were courage, loyalty, honour, courtesy, service to the church and protection of the weak. The 'seven perfections' included riding, swimming, archery, fencing, hunting, chess and verse-making. It was largely physical and social, with little intellectual education.
section-93: Dr. Zakir Hussain (1897-1969) was a co-founder of Jamia Millia Islamia, chairman of the committee that formulated the Wardha Scheme of Basic Education (1937-38), and later the third President of India.

He believed in education through productive craft, the development of character, cooperation and social service, and education in the mother tongue. Education should make the individual a useful member of a democratic society and develop moral and spiritual values.
section-94: Dr. Muhammad Iqbal (1877-1938) was a poet-philosopher whose central concept was 'Khudi' (selfhood). He believed that education should strengthen the self through action, courage, love, faith and creative activity.

His educational ideas include character building, dynamism, freedom, development of individuality in harmony with society, and synthesis of religious and modern scientific knowledge. He opposed passive imitation and stressed self-reliance.
section-95: Sri Aurobindo (1872-1950) founded an ashram at Pondicherry (Puducherry); the Sri Aurobindo International Centre of Education was developed there with the Mother. He gave three principles of teaching: (1) nothing can be taught - the teacher is a helper and guide; (2) the mind should be consulted in its growth; (3) work from the near to the far.

Integral education has five aspects - physical, vital, mental, psychic and spiritual. It aims at the evolution of the whole being and the realisation of the divine in man. He emphasised the mother tongue, freedom and individual differences.
section-96: Swami Vivekananda (1863-1902) said, 'Education is the manifestation of the perfection already in man.' He advocated man-making and character-building education, which develops strength, fearlessness, self-confidence and service to humanity.

He emphasised concentration of mind as the essence of education, the guru-shishya relationship, women's education, mass education, education for the poor, the combination of spiritual and scientific knowledge, and physical fitness. His birthday, 12 January, is celebrated as National Youth Day.
section-97: In 'Emile' (1762), Rousseau described the education of a child according to nature in stages: infancy (0-5, physical development), childhood (5-12, negative education and sense training), boyhood (12-15, intellectual education through experience) and adolescence (15-20, moral and social education).

Contributions: child-centred education, the concept of negative education, learning by doing, discipline by natural consequences, freedom, and respect for the child's individuality. He influenced Pestalozzi, Froebel, Montessori and Dewey.
section-98: Herbert Spencer (1820-1903), an English philosopher, asked 'What knowledge is of most worth?' and answered 'Science'. In 'Education: Intellectual, Moral and Physical' (1861), he described education as preparation for complete living.

He ranked activities in order of importance: (1) self-preservation (physiology, hygiene), (2) securing the necessities of life (vocational sciences), (3) rearing of children (parenthood), (4) social and political activities (citizenship), and (5) leisure (arts and literature). He advocated discipline by natural consequences and learning from simple to complex.
section-99: Bertrand Russell (1872-1970), British philosopher and Nobel laureate, wrote 'On Education' (1926) and 'Education and the Social Order' (1932). He founded Beacon Hill School with his wife Dora.

He emphasised four qualities to be developed by education: vitality, courage, sensitiveness and intelligence. He favoured freedom with discipline, scientific outlook, critical thinking, international understanding and peace, and opposed indoctrination, fear and blind nationalism.
section-100: Alfred North Whitehead (1861-1947), British mathematician and philosopher, wrote 'The Aims of Education' (1929). He criticised 'inert ideas' - ideas merely received into the mind without being used, tested or connected.

He described the rhythm of education in three stages: romance (excitement and discovery), precision (systematic and exact knowledge) and generalisation (application and synthesis). He advocated education that is useful, related to life, and develops both culture and expert knowledge.
section-102: Spartan education: A state-controlled system aiming at strong soldiers and obedient citizens. Boys from seven lived in barracks and underwent rigorous physical and military training; intellectual education was neglected. It produced discipline and patriotism but suppressed individuality.

Athenian education: Aimed at harmonious development of body and mind for democratic citizenship. Boys attended the palaestra and didascaleum and later received ephebic training. Philosophers like Socrates, Plato and Aristotle developed higher learning. Athens gave the ideal of liberal education.
Early Roman education (up to 275 BC): Family-centred and practical, teaching farming, warfare, law (Twelve Tables), religion and moral virtues through imitation and apprenticeship.

Later Roman education (275 BC-529 AD): Under Greek influence, Rome developed the ludus, grammar school and rhetoric school; Quintilian described the ideal orator. Roman education gave Europe the Latin language, law and an organised school system.
section-103: Monastic education: Starting with St. Benedict (529 AD), monasteries taught religion, Latin, reading, writing and the seven liberal arts, and preserved classical learning by copying manuscripts.
Scholasticism: From the 11th to 14th centuries, scholars like Abelard and Aquinas used logic and disputation to harmonise faith and reason, laying intellectual foundations for universities.

Medieval universities: Bologna, Paris, Salerno, Oxford and Cambridge emerged as self-governing communities of teachers and students with faculties of arts, theology, law and medicine and a system of degrees.

Education for chivalry: The nobility trained boys as pages, squires and finally knights in manners, arms, horsemanship and the ideals of courage, loyalty, courtesy and service. Medieval education thus combined religious, intellectual and social goals.
section-104: Zakir Hussain: He advocated craft-centred Basic Education (Wardha Scheme), character building, social service and education in the mother tongue.
Muhammad Iqbal: His philosophy of Khudi stressed development of the self through action, creativity, faith and moral strength, along with synthesis of religious and scientific knowledge.

Sri Aurobindo: His integral education aims at physical, vital, mental, psychic and spiritual development, guided by principles that the teacher is a helper and the mind should be consulted in its growth.

Swami Vivekananda: His man-making education emphasised character, strength, concentration, service, mass and women's education and a blend of spirituality and science. These thinkers enriched Indian educational thought with ideals of self-development, values and social responsibility.
section-105: Rousseau: The father of naturalism in education, he advocated child-centred education according to the stages of natural development, negative education, freedom and discipline by natural consequences.
Herbert Spencer: He defined education as preparation for complete living and gave first place to scientific knowledge, ranking life activities from self-preservation to leisure.
Bertrand Russell: He emphasised vitality, courage, sensitiveness and intelligence, freedom of thought, scientific outlook and international peace, opposing indoctrination.

A.N. Whitehead: He criticised inert ideas and proposed the rhythm of romance, precision and generalisation, so that knowledge remains alive and useful. These Western thinkers influenced modern child-centred, scientific and liberal education.
section-108: ECCE covers children from birth to about 8 years, the period when about 85 per cent of brain development takes place. It includes care (health, nutrition, safety) and education (play-based learning, language, social and cognitive development).
NEP 2020 gives high priority to ECCE and includes three years of pre-school in the Foundational Stage. The National ECCE Policy (2013) and NCF for the Foundational Stage (2022) provide frameworks.
section-109: Objectives: (1) physical development - motor skills, health and nutrition; (2) emotional development - security, confidence and expression of feelings; (3) social development - cooperation, sharing and good habits; (4) language development - listening, speaking, pre-reading and pre-writing; (5) cognitive development - curiosity, observation, concepts of number, colour and shape; (6) creative and aesthetic development; (7) school readiness.
ECCE also aims to reduce dropout and improve learning in primary school and to free older girls from sibling care so they can attend school.
section-110: NPE 1986 described ECCE as a crucial input for primary education and human resource development. It emphasised a holistic approach covering nutrition, health and social, mental, physical, moral and emotional development.

It recommended play-based, child-centred ECCE, avoidance of formal teaching of 3Rs at this stage, community involvement, integration with ICDS, and the establishment of day-care centres to support girls' education.
section-111: The Yash Pal Committee report 'Learning Without Burden' (1993) criticised the burden of non-understanding in schools. Regarding early childhood education, it recommended that formal teaching, tests and interviews for admission of young children should be abolished.

It recommended that pre-school education should be play-based and activity-based, children should not carry heavy school bags or be given homework at the pre-primary stage, and that the mother tongue should be used. It also emphasised training of pre-school teachers and regulation of private nursery schools.
section-112: Major programmes: Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS, 1975), now part of Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, providing supplementary nutrition, immunisation, health check-ups, referral services, pre-school education and nutrition and health education; balwadis; crèches under the National Creche Scheme; pre-primary classes in government schools under Samagra Shiksha.
Private nursery schools, kindergartens, Montessori schools and NGO programmes also provide ECCE. Health programmes include Mission Indradhanush (immunisation) and Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram.
section-113: The Indian Council for Child Welfare was founded in 1952 as a voluntary organisation. It has state branches across India.

Functions: running crèches, balwadis and pre-schools; training child welfare workers and pre-school teachers; organising National Bravery Awards for children; running programmes for street children, child labour and disabled children; promoting child rights and publishing materials on child welfare.
section-114: The Central Social Welfare Board was set up in 1953 under the leadership of Durgabai Deshmukh to promote social welfare activities through voluntary organisations.

Functions: giving grants to voluntary organisations for programmes for women and children, running welfare extension projects, condensed courses of education for adult women, crèches for working mothers, family counselling centres, and awareness generation programmes. State Social Welfare Boards work at the state level.
section-115: Nursery schools cater to children aged about 2 to 5 years. The nursery school movement was developed by Margaret and Rachel McMillan in England in the early 20th century, emphasising health, hygiene, open-air activities and nurturing.

Activities include free play, songs, stories, art, outdoor games, rest and meals. The nursery teacher acts like a mother and guide. Nursery education helps children develop good habits, social skills and readiness for school.
section-116: The kindergarten ('children's garden') was founded by Friedrich Froebel in Germany in 1837. He compared the school to a garden, the child to a plant and the teacher to a gardener.

Froebel's methods include 'gifts' (balls, cubes, cylinders, blocks) and 'occupations' (paper folding, clay modelling, weaving, drawing), songs, stories and games ('Mother Play and Nursery Songs'). Principles: self-activity, play, social participation and creativity. The kindergarten idea spread worldwide.
section-117: Dr. Maria Montessori (1870-1952), an Italian physician, opened the first 'Casa dei Bambini' (Children's House) in Rome in 1907. Her method is based on the child's natural desire to learn, sensitive periods and the 'absorbent mind'.

Features: prepared environment with child-sized furniture; didactic (self-correcting) apparatus for sense training; exercises of practical life (dressing, cleaning, pouring); auto-education; individual freedom; the teacher as directress who observes and guides. Criticism: it is costly and somewhat neglects imagination and group activities.
section-118: Anganwadi literally means 'courtyard shelter'. It is the basic unit of ICDS, run by an Anganwadi worker and helper, usually serving a population of about 400-800 in rural areas.

Services: supplementary nutrition, pre-school non-formal education for children aged 3-6, immunisation, health check-ups and referral (in coordination with the health department), and nutrition and health education for women. Under NEP 2020, Anganwadis are being strengthened with better infrastructure, play equipment and trained workers to deliver quality ECCE.
section-119: Programme planning involves deciding objectives, selecting activities, arranging a daily routine (arrival, free play, circle time, outdoor play, meals, rest, story time, departure), preparing materials, organising space (activity corners like reading, art, blocks and dolls), and evaluating children's progress.
Good planning balances active and quiet activities, indoor and outdoor play, individual and group activities, and teacher-guided and child-initiated activities.
section-120: Principles: (1) child-centred and developmentally appropriate; (2) holistic - covering all domains of development; (3) play-based and activity-based; (4) flexible and responsive to children's interests; (5) balanced; (6) based on local culture, language and resources; (7) inclusive; (8) involving parents and community; (9) continuous observation and assessment without formal tests.
Planning should move from simple to complex and from known to unknown and allow children to learn through exploration and experience.
section-121: Long-term planning covers a year or a term. It sets overall goals for development, selects themes for each month (such as myself, my family, animals, plants, seasons, festivals, transport), plans special events and outings, and allocates resources.
It provides direction and continuity and ensures that all areas of development are covered over the year.
section-122: Short-term or theme-based planning covers a week or a few days around a theme like 'fruits' or 'rain'. Activities across areas are linked to the theme: stories and rhymes about fruits (language), counting fruits (numeracy), drawing and colouring fruits (art), tasting and sorting (sensory and science), and role play of a fruit shop (social skills).
Theme-based planning integrates learning, maintains children's interest and connects learning to daily life.
section-123: Examples: bottle caps and seeds for counting; old boxes for building blocks; cloth and paper for puppets; old newspapers and magazines for collage; plastic bottles for musical shakers; leaves, stones and sticks for sorting and nature activities; clay from the local area for modelling.
Benefits: low cost, easy availability, environmental awareness (reuse), creativity of teachers and children, and connection with local culture. Materials must be safe, clean and non-toxic.
section-124: Children should be helped to develop self-help skills such as washing hands, using the toilet, eating independently, dressing, keeping belongings in place and cleanliness habits. Regular meals, rest and a safe environment are necessary.
These routines build independence, confidence and good habits. Teachers should be patient and encouraging, and coordinate with parents to maintain consistency between home and school.
section-125: Stories may be told using puppets, pictures, flannel boards, gestures and voice modulation. Folk tales, animal stories and local stories are popular with young children.

Benefits: develops listening skills and attention span, vocabulary and language, imagination and creativity, moral values, understanding of sequence and cause-effect, and emotional expression. Children can be encouraged to retell stories and act them out.
section-126: Nursery rhymes are short, rhythmic poems with repetition and actions, such as 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star', and local rhymes in the mother tongue.

Benefits: they develop phonological awareness (sounds and rhythm), vocabulary, memory, pronunciation, motor coordination (through actions), group participation and joy in learning. Rhymes in the mother tongue connect children to their culture.
section-127: Examples: block building, sand and water play, clay modelling, puzzles, beads threading, colouring and painting, cutting and pasting, playing with dolls and kitchen sets, and simple science materials like magnets.
Benefits: development of fine and gross motor skills, eye-hand coordination, concepts of size, shape, colour and number, creativity, problem-solving and social skills through sharing.
section-128: Examples: running, jumping, hopping, dancing, action songs, imitation games (walking like animals), circle games, hide and seek, 'Simon says', finger play, dramatisation and traditional games.

Benefits: physical fitness and gross motor development, listening and following instructions, social skills, cooperation, rule-following, self-expression and imagination. Such activities are especially useful where materials are scarce.
